newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Over 1,000 Angolan villagers flee unrest, officials.
newsitem.headline: Over 1,000 Angolan villagers flee unrest, officials.

text.p: Over 1,000 people in southwestern Angola have fled their villages over the past two days because of unrest in the area, aid officials said on Sunday.
"Violence in this region has been endemic for some time, but this is on a different scale," an aid group director in the city of Lubango told Reuters.

A column of people, mainly from the village of Yambala, started arriving in the city of Cubal in Benguela province on Saturday, aid workers said. The city already hosts some 120,000 people displaced by Angola's two-decade-long civil war.
The refugees did not tell aid workers who was reponsible for the unrest but spoke of villages being set on fire and of scores injured in attacks.

"It's a very confusing situation at the moment. It is impossible to say exactly how many people have arrived in Cubal but our people there say more than 1,500," said Catherine Quillet of the medical aid group Medecins Sans Frontiers, from her home in Luanda.

"We know the refugees walked about 10 hours to get to Cubal from Yambala. They are saying their villages were burned down by men who were wearing uniforms. Whether these men are UNITA or government troops or someone else, we don't know," she said.

The area around Yambala used to be controlled by the former UNITA rebel movement but has recently come under the control of locally organised civil defence units who are supported by the government, according to aid workers and other officials there.
Some reports suggest that renegade UNITA troops have moved back into the area to try to establish their influence.

The area around Cubal and Yambala has historically been one of Angola's most unstable areas. A highway linking the Atlantic port of Benguela, and running through Cubal to the highland city of Huambo, is known as dangerous with "regular" and renegade troops from both sides.

Officials say the unrest in Benguela underlines the deep problems that Angola still has to overcome to effectively end a civil war that erupted between the government and UNITA movement in 1975 after independence from Portugal.
The two sides signed a peace accord in the Zambian capital Lusaka in 1994 but a formal ending of hostilities and the establishment of a unity government have yet to be implemented.

"This unrest is nothing new but it is disturbing, especially at a time when we are trying to bring about official government administration to these areas," an official close to the peace process told Reuters.

"This is a sign that what is happening here in Luanda -- the progress we are making in the peace process -- has not extended to the grassroots level," he said. "At that level there is still a lot of tension, still very much a struggle for control."
